office.title: Indiana School Board Member
office.summary: A school board is the elected or appointed governing body of a public school corporation, the legal unit that runs a local school district [1, 2]. The board hires and evaluates the superintendent, adopts policies, and approves the annual budget, while the superintendent and staff run schools day to day [3]. Most boards have five or seven members serving staggered four-year terms [3]. Starting in 2026, candidates may list a political party, run as independents, or list no affiliation on the ballot, and there is no primary for these seats [2, 4].

facts.label: Term
facts.value: 4 years, with elections staggered so part of the board is chosen every two years [3]

facts.label: Elected
facts.value: At the November general election (November 3, 2026, or November 2028 for some seats); depending on the local organization plan, members represent the whole school corporation (at large) or a district within it, and some boards are wholly or partly appointed [2]

facts.label: Ballot label
facts.value: Each candidate chooses a party label, 'Independent', or no affiliation, shown next to the name; no primary and no straight-ticket voting for these races [2, 4]

facts.label: Pay
facts.value: Set by board resolution: an annual amount of no more than 10% of the lowest starting teacher salary in the school corporation, plus a capped per diem [5]

duties: Hires, evaluates and can dismiss the superintendent, and approves the hiring and firing of principals, teachers and other staff recommended by the superintendent [1, 7, 3].
Adopts the annual budget, appropriates funds and oversees school finances [1, 3].

Decides whether to ask voters to approve an operating referendum (an extra property tax levy); the board adopts the resolution and the Department of Local Government Finance reviews the ballot language for compliance with state law [8].
Approves contracts, buys and sells property, and decides on construction, repair and demolition of school buildings [1].

Bargains with the teachers' union over salary, wages and wage-related benefits such as health insurance and retirement; state law excludes teacher evaluation procedures from those bargaining subjects [9].
Writes and updates policies and rules for schools, often in a policy handbook, including the student handbook [1, 3].
Buys curricular materials, provides them to students without charge, and runs programs such as student transportation and school lunch [1].

Must adopt a process for parents and residents to ask that library material be removed as obscene or harmful to minors, review requests at public meetings and keep a public catalog of library materials [10].
Hears written appeals of student expulsions, unless the board has voted not to hear them [11].
Must take official action openly; Indiana's Open Door Law says public agencies' official action is to be conducted openly so the people may be fully informed [12, 13].

A school board member must have lived in the school corporation (and, for a district seat, the district) for at least one year before the election, and a teacher or other employee of the school corporation may not serve on its board [2].

What the board does not control: the State Board of Education adopts statewide academic standards [14], the General Assembly sets the state school funding formula in the state budget [15], and voucher (Choice Scholarship) eligibility is set by state law [16].
recent_changes: 2025: Senate Enrolled Act 287 allowed school board candidates to declare a party affiliation; the Indiana School Boards Association opposed the change, and a supporter quoted by WNDU, a Noblesville school board member, said it adds transparency [17].

2026: Candidates choose a party, 'Independent' or no affiliation on their nominating petition, and that choice appears on the ballot; a candidate claiming the Democratic or Republican party must have voted in that party's primary in the two most recent primaries they voted in, or have certification from the county party chair, or can be challenged and removed from the ballot [2].

July 2026: Chalkbeat reported, citing Indiana School Boards Association data, that 524 of 1,044 candidates chose a party, about 72% of them Republicans [18]; the Indiana Election Division's 2026 guidance and the wording of the law differ on the primary-voting test, a question county election boards decide [19].

February 2026: Senate Enrolled Act 25 set the order of school board candidates on the ballot, grouped by party, with candidates who list no affiliation placed after the party and independent candidates [20].

2025: Senate Enrolled Act 1, a property tax law, limits how much operating revenue districts can raise through taxes and restricts school referendums to statewide general elections in even-numbered years [21, 22].
2025: The same law requires districts to share operating revenue with brick-and-mortar charter schools that enroll their students, statewide starting in 2028 [21, 22].
2025: The state budget opened Choice Scholarship vouchers to all Indiana families starting in June 2026 [16].
2026: The Indianapolis Public Education Corporation, rather than the Indianapolis Public Schools board, now certifies Indianapolis Public Schools referendum questions for the ballot [20].

2023: Senate Enrolled Act 391 changed the so-called $1 law so the Indiana Department of Education can order districts that lost at least 10% of enrollment over five years to close schools under 60% capacity and offer them to charter schools [23].
2023: House Enrolled Act 1447 required school districts to set up procedures for complaints that library material is obscene or harmful to minors [10].

race_context: The district: the 'Morgan MSD Martinsville School Board' seat belongs to the Metropolitan School District of Martinsville (MSD of Martinsville) in Morgan County, based in Martinsville [24, 25]. The district lists seven K-4 elementary schools, Bell Intermediate Academy (grades 5-6), John R. Wooden Middle School, Martinsville High School, Hammons Alternative School and preschool programs [26]. Federal data list 3,998 students in ten schools in 2024-25 [24]. Dr. Eric Bowlen is superintendent; the board selected him effective July 1, 2022, after he served as a middle school principal and then Martinsville High School principal [26, 25].

The board has five members: Luke Jackson (president), Dan Conway (vice president), Matt Hankins (secretary), Jacque Deckard and Heather Staggs [27]. State election results list five numbered districts with one seat each; Districts 1, 3 and 4 were on the ballot in 2020 and 2024, and Districts 2 and 5 in 2022 [28, 29, 30]. This guide did not find the district's own description of residence rules or of which voters may vote in each district race.

Seat on the 2026 ballot: District 2, which elects one member, matching the state list's 'vote for 1' [6, 29]. Dan Conway holds the seat: he won it in 2022 with 4,051 votes to 3,700 for incumbent Don Lipps [29]. Conway is running for re-election and is challenged by Jordan Scott Terrell [6].

District 5, held by board president Luke Jackson since he won it unopposed in 2022, would also normally be up in 2026, but no District 5 race appears on the state list [29, 6, 27]. This guide could not determine why.
Party labels: both candidates are listed as Republicans on the state list [6]. In 2022 the District 2 candidates ran without party labels [31, 29].

Elementary consolidation: the district plans to close Centerton Elementary, Green Township Elementary, Poston Road Elementary and Smith Fine Arts Academy at the end of the 2026-27 school year and open one new elementary school for 2027-28, according to a December 2025 district announcement published by the Martinsville Chamber of Commerce [32]. The district said all four buildings were built before the 1960s and that maintaining several aging buildings costs more than building and operating one new school; it described the project as tax-neutral, built under a 'Build-Operate-Transfer' model [32, 33]. The announcement said the board was scheduled to approve the plans on December 10, 2025; this guide did not find a record of that vote [32]. Then-board president Heather Staggs said the board's responsibility is to 'plan not just for today's students, but for generations to come' [33].

Bond projects: in May 2026 the district sought proposals for a $12.5 million package of smaller projects funded by general obligation bonds, including a gym roof at John R. Wooden Middle School, HVAC and other upgrades at Poston Road Elementary, Martinsville High School auditorium and cafeteria work, playground and furniture upgrades at four elementary schools, demolition at Charles L. Smith Fine Arts Academy, and solar at Paragon Elementary and the high school [25].

Budget and taxes: the 2027 budget hearing was set for October 8, 2026 and adoption for October 22, 2026 [34]. The published notice lists a $61.3 million total budget estimate; for the debt service fund it lists a maximum of $12,531,898 to be raised, 42.27 percent above the current levy of $8,808,726, and an estimated $946,000 in property-tax cap credits [34]. This guide found no public statement from the board on how the 2025 property-tax law (SEA 1) affects Martinsville's budget. Martinsville is not listed among districts with referendums on the November 2026 ballot [35].

Teacher pay: in October 2025 the Indiana Department of Education notified the district that its state tuition support rose from fiscal 2024 to 2025 but that it did not meet the state's minimum spending requirement for full-time teacher salaries, spending $14,227,991.79 against a required floor of $14,630,676.84; the district was required to acknowledge the notice at a public meeting and post it online [36].
Board meeting minutes are posted on BoardDocs, which could not be read for this guide, so individual votes in 2025-26 are not described here [27].
Forums and questionnaires: this guide found no 2026 candidate forum, newspaper questionnaire or VOTE411 entry for this race.

candidates.summary: Incumbent and board vice president, first elected in 2022 [29, 27].
background: Won the District 2 seat in 2022, defeating incumbent Don Lipps [29, 37].
path_to_ballot: Listed as a Republican on the state list [6].

items: As a 2022 candidate, named bullying as a challenge for the district: 'I've heard a lot of concerns from different folks about the bullying, about how we report it and then what are we doing to correct it,' and said he was meeting with a district to see how it handles and reports bullying [37].

In 2022 said the district should find out why families who live in the MSD send their children elsewhere, saying he had asked parents at other schools, 'What is your negative to Martinsville?', and that the district should address their concerns with 'more of an action plan' [37].

on_incumbent: Is a current board member and the board's vice president [27].
As a challenger in 2022, said families he talked to were frustrated with the MSD of Martinsville [37]. No 2026 account of the board's record from him was found.
gaps: No campaign website, questionnaire, forum answers or 2026 news coverage found; positions above are from his 2022 campaign.
Occupation and other background not found.
No 2026 statements found on the elementary consolidation, the 2026 bond projects, the teacher-salary funding-floor notice, the budget or SEA 1.
His votes on 2025-26 board decisions could not be checked because the district's BoardDocs minutes were not readable.
